title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can support automated scoring and feedback for middle-school mathematics open-response items. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned Mistral-based model called GOAT, the prior SBERT-Canberra similarity-based method, and GPT-4 used in zero-shot mode with a grading rubric. The main questions are whether these models can predict teacher scores accurately and which model produces the most useful feedback for student responses.

The study uses student responses to open-ended math problems drawn from an online learning platform, specifically from a group of about 50 teachers who used open-ended questions in their classrooms. The dataset is filtered to language-based problems only and includes 50 math problems with 100 student responses each. The models are evaluated on held-out test data using AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa for scoring, and two human evaluators with teaching experience rate feedback for accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preference.

Quantitatively, GOAT performs best on score prediction, outperforming SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on all scoring metrics. Qualitatively, however, GPT-4 produces the most accurate, relevant, motivating, and preferred feedback according to the human raters. The authors conclude that fine-tuned open-source LLMs can improve automated scoring, but that GPT-4 currently generates stronger educational feedback. They also note tradeoffs: GOAT inherits weaknesses from imperfect teacher-written feedback in its training data, while GPT-4’s stronger feedback quality comes from its broader pretraining rather than task-specific adaptation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative model-evaluation study with a held-out test split and human ratings, but it is not an experimental study of student learning outcomes. Evidence is useful and reasonably systematic, yet primarily technical/qualitative rather than a rigorous causal educational evaluation.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but modest practical impact for teacher-facing automation, especially for scoring and feedback workflow support. However, it does not demonstrate student achievement gains, and the evidence is limited to model performance and human preference judgments rather than classroom impact.

interventions.use_case: automated scoring and feedback generation for middle-school students' open-ended math responses using fine-tuned LLMs and an LLM baseline

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates whether AI can automate scoring and feedback generation for open-ended middle-school math responses, which would reduce teacher grading workload. GOAT achieved the best scoring performance (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422) on 1,000 held-out responses, suggesting improved efficiency for auto-scoring relative to SBERT and GPT-4. Human evaluators also judged GPT-4 and GOAT-generated feedback as usable starting points, indicating potential workflow support for teachers.
finding.measure: Auto-scoring accuracy (AUC, RMSE, Cohen's Kappa) and human-rated feedback usefulness/preference
finding.study_size: n=5000 responses total; n=1000 test responses for scoring; n=100 sampled responses for feedback review
